title: Two Kinds of Searching

post.author: u/night_phones_bryher
post.title: I answer the night phones for a missing-persons charity. Our archive's assistant couldn't find a woman by her own name. It found her coat instead, in a report nobody had linked to her since 1999.

blocks.text: On Thursdays I volunteer on the night helpline at the Lanternline Trust, a missing-persons charity, from ten until six. Behind the phones sits our archive: case files, sighting reports and letters going back decades, all typed up. Since the spring we search it through an assistant, a program that does vector search only: it turns my words into a list of numbers that stands for their meaning, and fetches the files whose numbers sit closest.
The old keyword search box from 2012 is still on the server, the computer that holds the archive. It looks for the exact words you type. Nobody uses it.

At 23:52 a man rang and asked whether anyone had ever found his aunt. He gave her surname, Gorrimer, and her case number, 98/0417. I typed both into the assistant. Each line below shows the time, the place a file came in the results, the file, and its score: how close the assistant thinks it is, where 1 would be a perfect match.

23:52  search  Gorrimer 98/0417
23:52  1  Margaret Gorman, 97/0388    0.929
       2  Rowena Gormley, 99/0102    0.898
       3  Wilfrida Gorringe, 97/0211    0.859
Three women. None of them his aunt.

Zillah Greaves, our archivist until 2014, kept a card index, one paper card per person, filed by surname, and her drawers still stand under the window. Drawer G had her in seconds: GORRIMER, Juliet, 98/0417. I tried the old keyword box with the same search. Her file came first, the only match.

Conal Lightfoot, a retired police dog handler, volunteers on Thursdays too. He read her file aloud: last seen in a long yellow raincoat with horn toggles, and she spoke of walking to St Cleave's Light. Then he typed that description into the assistant. First, at 0.997, came a sighting report, a note from a stranger who saw someone, from Saltrigg, in the next county, November 1999: a woman in a mustard duffel coat asked the ferryman which way was the old lighthouse at Garrow Head. Conal says Garrow Head is what Saltrigg calls St Cleave's Light.
The keyword box put that report fifth for the same words. The assistant's screen shows only the top three.

blocks.label: two_searches_thursday.png

diagram.aria: Bryher's drawing of Thursday's two searches. Left, Gorrimer 98/0417: the assistant's top 3 were Margaret Gorman 0.929, Rowena Gormley 0.898 and Wilfrida Gorringe 0.859; Juliet Gorrimer's file came 4th at 0.745 and was not shown; the keyword box put her file 1st at 4.99, the only match. Right, Conal's description: the assistant put the Saltrigg sighting of 1999 1st at 0.997; the keyword box put it 5th at 1.53, sharing only the words woman and in, under her file 12.81, a 2003 letter 3.44 and Lachlan Hartsop's file 2.35.

blocks.caption: Drawn on Friday morning from Thursday's two searches. Left, the caller's search: the assistant's top 3 were three other women; her own file came 4th at 0.745 and was never shown, and the keyword box found it 1st at 4.99. Right, Conal's description: the assistant put the Saltrigg report 1st at 0.997; the keyword box put it 5th at 1.53, under her file at 12.81, a letter of 2003 at 3.44, Lachlan Hartsop's file at 2.35 and Wilfrida Gorringe's at 2.30.

blocks.text: The archive forgot her name but remembered her coat. The two halves of her case have sat in the same archive for 27 years and never met. The trustees, the people who run the charity, want one search box by next month. What do I change?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing in your archive forgot anyone. The two boxes are two kinds of search. Your assistant does vector search. First it embeds your words: it turns them into an embedding, a list of numbers that stands for their meaning. Every document was embedded the same way ahead of time. Then it compares your list with each document's and returns the nearest, measured by cosine similarity (a closeness score that tops out at 1). The 2012 box does keyword search. It looks up which documents hold your exact words, then scores them with BM25, the scoring from Dead Letter's Word Index case. In BM25, rare words weigh most, so a word few files contain counts for a lot. Each result list is ranked: best first, so a file's rank is its place, 1 for first. Two questions. For Gorrimer 98/0417, where did her own file come in the assistant's list, with its score? And for Conal's description, where did the keyword box put the Saltrigg report, and which of your words does it actually contain?

replies.author: u/night_phones_bryher
replies.text: Her file came fourth, at 0.745, under Margaret Gorman 0.929, Rowena Gormley 0.898 and Wilfrida Gorringe 0.859; the assistant shows three. In the keyword box the Saltrigg report came fifth, at 1.53, under her file 12.81, a 2003 letter 3.44, Lachlan Hartsop's file 2.35 and Wilfrida Gorringe's 2.30. Of Conal's words it contains two: woman and in. Raincoat, yellow, toggles and Cleave's aren't in it. It says duffel coat, mustard and Garrow Head.

comments.author: u/vectors_know_wrexley
comments.text: Embeddings understand everything; keyword search is legacy, old stuff kept running. Your assistant found a report from another county that shares two words with her file. No keyword index (the word-to-files list behind the old box) will ever do that. The name miss is a model problem. You're on a small, cheap embedding model, the program that makes the lists of numbers, and a bigger one keeps rare names and numbers apart. Don't bolt the 2012 box back on. And don't let anyone sell you hybrid search either: running both searches on the same words, then merging the two lists into one. They'll merge them with something called reciprocal rank fusion. It goes in steps. Each file gets points from its place in each list, more for a higher place. The points from both lists are added. Then the files are sorted by the total. That's two systems to keep in step for a problem a better model solves.

replies.author: u/night_phones_bryher
replies.text: The assistant came with the model the Trust could afford. What would a bigger one change for a number like 98/0417?

replies.author: u/vectors_know_wrexley
replies.text: Everything. Upgrade once and forget the old box.

comments.author: u/drawer_g_zillah
comments.text: I filed people by surname and sightings by the place they came from. The Saltrigg report has been under S since the day it came in, because it had no name on it. I never cross-filed sightings from another county, putting a second card under a missing person's name. My drawers could find anyone by name in seconds, and nobody could ever ask them for a yellow coat.

replies.author: u/night_phones_bryher
replies.text: Your card for her is still in drawer G. I've put a copy of the Saltrigg report behind it.

comments.author: u/scent_and_lead_conal
comments.text: A bloodhound is given something the person wore, and it follows that. A name means nothing to a dog. St Cleave's Light is the Wetherdene name; across the estuary, where the river meets the sea, they call it the Garrow Head light. We walked the Wetherdene shore below it with two dogs in March 1998 and lost the scent at the water. Nobody told us about Saltrigg.

reply.prompt: The trustees want one search box by next month. What should Bryher change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Keep vector search only, but switch to a bigger embedding model that keeps rare names well apart.
options.part2: The trustees paid for a larger embedding model, and Bryher embedded the archive again over a weekend. Zillah wrote six test questions whose right files she knew: two names, two case numbers and two descriptions. The assistant passed the same 2 of 6 as before, both descriptions. For Rowena Gormley it put Margaret Gorman's file first; for 97/0211 it put Lachlan Hartsop's first and Wilfrida Gorringe's own file fourth. Gorrimer 98/0417 still opened on three other women.
options.senior: Embeddings place text by meaning, and a rare surname or a case number carries almost none, so even a larger model usually lands it beside names and numbers that look alike. Exact labels such as names and case numbers need exact matching: keyword search beside the vectors, not a bigger model instead of it.

options.text: Go back to keyword search only, plus a hand-made list of other words for coats, colours and places.
options.verdict: Only the words you thought of
options.part2: Bryher switched the archive back to the keyword box, and with Zillah she wrote a synonym list, other words that count as a match: raincoat also searches coat, yellow also searches mustard. Conal's description now put the Saltrigg report second, at 4.29, under her file. Zillah's six test questions: 5 of 6. The one it missed was the letter of 2003 about a porch light kept on every night. The search lamp left burning for lost daughter shares no word with it, and found nothing at all.
options.senior: A synonym list helps where you can guess the words in advance. But descriptions are paraphrase, the same meaning in other words, and nobody can list every way to say a thing. That is the job vectors do well. Keep a list for known variants such as old place names, and let vectors carry the rest.

options.text: Run both searches, merge them by reciprocal rank fusion, and test on questions with known files.
options.part2: Bryher put the 2012 keyword index back beside the assistant and merged the two lists by reciprocal rank fusion, k = 60. (k is a number added to each place before the points are worked out; it keeps first place from counting too much.) At first she took the top 3 from each list, since the screen shows three. Zillah's six test questions caught it: for 97/0211, Margaret Gorman's file came first at 0.0317, third in both lists, and Wilfrida Gorringe's own file second at 0.0164, first for keywords but fourth for vectors, outside the window of places taken. With a rank window of 10, the top 10 from each list, Wilfrida's file came first at 0.0320, and all 6 passed. Gorrimer 98/0417 now opens on Juliet's file at 0.0320, and Conal's description puts the Saltrigg report second, at 0.0318, right under it. On Monday the Trust sent both to the police in Saltrigg.
options.senior: Keyword search usually wins on names, codes and exact phrases; vectors win on paraphrase and description. Run both and fuse by rank. BM25 scores have no fixed top and cosines never pass 1, so the scores can't be added fairly, but places can. Then test on known questions of each kind, because a window or a constant that looks harmless can push a sure hit down, and only a known answer shows it.

options.text: Show both result lists side by side, and let the volunteer read all six and pick the right file.
options.part2: The screen now shows two lists of three: keyword on the left, vectors on the right. Zillah's six test questions: the right file was in one list or the other every time, 6 of 6. But every question means six results to read, and the lists disagree. For Gorrimer 98/0417 the left opens on Juliet's file and the right on Margaret Gorman's. At 03:40 on a busy night, a new volunteer read the right-hand list first and told a caller there was nothing under the name he gave. It was first on the left.
options.senior: Two lists side by side work when someone careful reads both, and it is a fair first step. But it doubles the reading, gives no single order to trust, and leaves the merge to a tired person at 3 AM. Fusion, merging the lists by a fixed rule, makes that merge the same way every time, and you can test it.

sim.title: Search the Lanternline archive three ways
sim.lede: You're Bryher at 23:52 on Thursday, with a test archive of ten documents copied from the real one: six case files, the Saltrigg sighting report, two letters and a helpline rota. There is no real model and no real embedding. Keyword search scores with BM25 exactly as in the Word Index case (k1 1.2, b 0.75; the case number 98/0417 is two tokens, 98 and 0417). Vector search scores every document by cosine similarity of vectors stated by hand on five named dimensions: a case file, a name like Gor-, a yellow coat, the coast and the lighthouse, someone waiting at home. That is a teaching simplification; real embeddings have hundreds of unnamed dimensions. The stated vectors stand in for any embedding model, large or small: a rare name or a case number carries almost no meaning for either, so vector search only here is also what a bigger model gives. Hybrid search runs both and merges them by reciprocal rank fusion: each file gets 1 / (k + rank) from each list, counting only the top results of each list up to a limit, the rank window, and a tie goes to the better keyword rank. The volunteer reads the top 3. Choose the search, the mode, k, the rank window, and a hand-made synonym list. The test set is six questions whose right files are known: a name or number passes when its right file comes first, a description when it is in the top 3.
sim.tryThis: Try this: you start as the assistant runs, vector search only. Margaret Gorman comes first at 0.929 and her file fourth at 0.745; the test set passes 2 of 6. Switch to keyword search: her file first at 4.99, 4 of 6. Pick Conal's description: the Saltrigg report is fifth at 1.53. Now hybrid: the report comes second at 0.0318, her file first, 6 of 6. Pick the test question 97/0211 and set the rank window to 3: Margaret Gorman's file, third in both lists, wins at 0.0317, and the test set drops to 5 of 6. Try k 10, 30 and 100: the window matters here, k barely does. Then keyword only with the synonym list: 5 of 6, and the lamp question finds nothing. Last, both lists side by side: 6 of 6, with six results to read.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in the archive forgot her. Vector search placed a rare name and a case number among names that look alike, keyword search couldn't see a description written in other words, and each search found the half of her case the other missed.

steps.title: Vector search blurred her name.
steps.text: Vector search goes in steps. First, every document is embedded ahead of time: turned into a list of numbers that stands for its meaning. Second, when a search comes in, its words are embedded the same way. Third, the search's list is compared with every document's by cosine similarity, a closeness score that tops out at 1. Last, the closest few are shown. What can go wrong is in the first two steps: a rare surname and a case number carry almost no meaning, so their numbers say little. Gorrimer 98/0417 landed among files with names like it: Margaret Gorman 0.929, Rowena Gormley 0.898, Wilfrida Gorringe 0.859. Her own file came fourth at 0.745, one place below what the screen shows. Embeddings are usually good with meaning and weak with exact strings of letters, codes and numbers.

steps.title: Keyword search found her, and missed her coat.
steps.text: Keyword search goes in steps too. First, the keyword index lists, for every word, the documents that hold it, like the index at the back of a book. Second, the search's words are looked up in it. Third, BM25 scores each document that holds them. It weighs rare words most, through inverse document frequency: the fewer documents hold a word, the more it counts. Gorrimer, 98 and 0417 are in her file alone, so it scored 4.99 and was the only match. Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval post says BM25 is particularly effective for queries (searches) that include unique identifiers (labels that name one thing) or technical terms. What can go wrong is the lookup: a word that isn't in a document can't match it. The Saltrigg report says mustard duffel coat and Garrow Head, not yellow raincoat and St Cleave's Light. It shares only woman and in, common words that weigh little, so it scored 1.53 and came fifth.

steps.title: Run both, and fuse the lists by rank.
steps.text: Hybrid search runs both searches on the same words and merges the two ranked lists. Reciprocal rank fusion does the merge in steps. First, take the top results of each list. Second, give each file 1 / (k + rank) from each list it appears in, where rank is its place and k is a fixed number, 60 in the 2009 paper by Cormack, Clarke and Büttcher. Third, add the file's points from both lists. Last, sort by the total. Her file, first for keywords and fourth for vectors, scores 1/61 + 1/64 = 0.0320; Margaret Gorman, first for vectors and absent from the keyword list, 1/61 = 0.0164. For Conal's description, the report, fifth and first, scores 1/65 + 1/61 = 0.0318, second, under her file. Fusion uses ranks because the scores don't share a scale, the range they fall in: BM25 gave 12.81 and 4.99, cosine never passes 1. The other way is weighted blending. It shrinks each search's scores to the same range, multiplies each by a weight, and adds them. That can work, but the weights need tuning: trying values until the results look right.

steps.title: The rank window can bury a sure hit.
steps.text: Only the top results of each list, the rank window, take part. A file that is first in one list and outside the other's window scores 1/61, about 0.0164, while a file fifth in both scores 2/65, about 0.0308. With a window of 3, the test question 97/0211 went wrong exactly this way: Margaret Gorman's file, third in both lists, scored 2/63 = 0.0317, and Wilfrida Gorringe's own file, first for keywords but fourth for vectors, only 0.0164. With a window of 5 or 10 her file comes first again, at 0.0320. Elasticsearch, a widely used search engine, has an RRF (reciprocal rank fusion) step that defaults to a window of 10 and k of 60.

steps.title: Test the fused list on known answers.
steps.text: Zillah's six questions are a retrieval test set: questions whose right files are marked in advance, so a search can be checked against them. It has each kind in it: two names, two case numbers, two descriptions. Testing goes in steps: run every question, see where its right file lands, and count the passes. Vector only passed 2 of 6, keyword only 4 of 6, keyword with a synonym list 5 of 6, fusion with a window of 3 passed 5 of 6, and fusion with a window of 10 passed all 6. The paper found k = 60 near-optimal but not critical, and here k changed nothing while the window did. Rerun the set whenever the window, k, the model or the documents change. Fusion only orders what the two searches return. Case 5 of this season adds a second, more careful look at the top results, called reranking.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for the caller's search. The search Gorrimer 98/0417 goes to two searches. Keyword search with BM25 puts her file first at 4.99; vector search with cosine similarity puts it fourth at 0.745, with a rank window of 10 from each. Reciprocal rank fusion adds 1 / (60 + rank) from each list: 1/61 + 1/64 = 0.0320, first. The fused list is checked by a test set of names, numbers and descriptions: 6 of 6.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for the caller's search. Both searches run on the same words, and the top 10 of each go into reciprocal rank fusion. Her file is first for keywords and fourth for vectors, so it scores 1/61 + 1/64 = 0.0320 and comes first. Six known questions, two of each kind, check the fused list whenever a setting changes.

fix.title: The fix: run both searches, fuse them by rank, and test on known answers
fix.text: Put the keyword index back beside the vectors and run every search through both. Merge the two lists by reciprocal rank fusion with k = 60, taking the top 10 from each list rather than the 3 the screen shows. Keep Zillah's six questions as a test set, two names, two case numbers and two descriptions, and add a question every time a search fails on the phones. Run the set before any change goes live: to the window, k, the embedding model or the analyzer (the steps that cut text into words for the keyword index). A name or number should come back first; a description should sit in the top 3.

limits: Fusion only reorders what the two searches return. A document neither list holds within its window can't be fused in, and a window that is too small can push a sure hit down, as 97/0211 showed at 3.

Reciprocal rank fusion ignores how sure each search was: a keyword match at 12.81 and one at 0.29 differ only by their places. Where one search is clearly better for a kind of question, weighted blending or a reranker (a slower model that rescores the top results) may do better, at the cost of tuning.

Two searches mean two indexes, two stores of the archive's words or numbers, to build, update and delete from, and more work per question. On a large archive the keyword index and the vectors have to stay in step, or one half answers from old data.

explain.seniorTake: Keyword search and vector search fail in opposite places: keyword search on the same meaning in other words, vector search on names, codes and numbers. Run both and merge by place in each list, so you never have to put BM25 scores and cosines on one scale. Then treat the merged list like code that must pass its tests: keep a test set with names, numbers and descriptions, and run it on every change. The settings that bury a sure hit, a file that should plainly come first, look harmless until a known answer moves.

realWorld.title: Cormack, Clarke and Büttcher, SIGIR 2009: k = 60
realWorld.text: The paper defines the score of a document as the sum over the rankings of 1 / (k + r(d)), and says k = 60 was fixed during a pilot investigation and not altered during subsequent validation. It adds that the constant k mitigates the impact of high rankings by outlier systems, and that its pilot results indicated k = 60 was near-optimal, but that the choice was not critical.

realWorld.title: Cormack, Clarke and Büttcher: the finding
realWorld.text: The abstract says Reciprocal Rank Fusion, a simple method for combining the document rankings from multiple IR systems (information retrieval, that is, search systems), consistently yields better results than any individual system, and better results than the standard method Condorcet Fuse (a merge by majority vote between each pair of documents).

realWorld.title: Elasticsearch: rank_constant defaults to 60
realWorld.text: Elastic's (the company behind the Elasticsearch search engine) reciprocal rank fusion page describes RRF as a method for combining multiple result sets, and says rank_constant determines how much influence documents in individual result sets per query have over the final ranked result set. It defaults to 60. Of rank_window_size, it says a higher value will improve result relevance at the cost of performance.

realWorld.title: Elasticsearch RRF retriever: a window of 10
realWorld.text: The RRF retriever's reference says rank_window_size determines the size of the individual result sets per query, and that it defaults to 10. Its hybrid search example combines a standard retriever (a keyword search step) with a knn retriever (a nearest-neighbour, vector search step) using RRF.

realWorld.title: Anthropic, 2024: where BM25 wins
realWorld.text: Anthropic's Introducing Contextual Retrieval post says BM25 uses lexical matching (matching the words themselves) to find precise word or phrase matches, and is particularly effective for queries that include unique identifiers or technical terms. Its example is a search for Error code TS-999, where an embedding model might find content about error codes in general but could miss the exact TS-999 match. The post's own method is case 7 of this season.

realWorld.title: pgvector: hybrid search in Postgres
realWorld.text: The pgvector README (the project's front page; pgvector adds vector search to the Postgres database) says to use it together with Postgres full-text search (its built-in keyword search) for hybrid search, and that you can use Reciprocal Rank Fusion or a cross-encoder (a model that reads the search and a document together and scores the pair) to combine results.

asked: What is hybrid search, and why use it?
How does reciprocal rank fusion work?
When does vector search fail where keyword search succeeds?
interview.answer: Hybrid search runs a keyword search, usually BM25, and a vector search over the same documents and merges the two ranked lists. You use it because they fail in opposite places. Vector search finds paraphrase and description: a mustard duffel coat for a yellow raincoat. But a rare surname, a case number, an error code or a product SKU (a shop's code for one product) carries little meaning, so its embedding lands near things that look alike, and the exact match can fall below the cut. BM25 finds those at once, because rare tokens weigh most, but it can't match words that aren't there. To merge, I'd use reciprocal rank fusion: each document scores the sum of 1 / (k + rank) over the lists, with k usually 60, counting the top N of each list, the rank window. It uses ranks because BM25 scores and cosine similarities aren't on a common scale, so adding raw scores lets one side swamp the other. The alternative is weighted blending: shrink both sets of scores to the same range, weight them and add them, which needs tuning. Then I'd watch the window: a sure hit that is first in one list and outside the other's window scores 1/61, below a file fifth in both at 2/65. So I keep a test set with names, numbers and descriptions, check that exact identifiers come back first, and rerun it whenever the window, k, the embedding model or the analyzer changes. Elasticsearch defaults to k 60 and a window of 10, and pgvector's README points to Postgres full-text search for the keyword half. Next I'd consider a reranker, a slower model that rescores the fused top results, if quality still falls short.

terms.def: A charity that helps families look for people who have gone missing: it keeps case records, takes sightings and runs a helpline. The Lanternline Trust is one.
A phone line people can ring for help. Lanternline's runs through the night, answered by volunteers such as Bryher.
The record a charity keeps on one missing person: who they are, when and where they were last seen, what they wore.
The reference given to a case file, such as 98/0417: the year, then a running number. A tokenizer splits it into two tokens, 98 and 0417.
A note of someone seen who may be a missing person, often by a stranger who doesn't know their name. The Saltrigg report of 1999 is one.
Paper cards in drawers, one per record, filed in an order such as by surname. Zillah's finds a name in seconds but can't be asked for a description.
The person who keeps an organization's records in order and helps people find them. Zillah Greaves was Lanternline's until 2014.
A police officer who works with a trained dog, such as a bloodhound that follows a person's scent from something they wore. Conal Lightfoot is retired.
A heavy coat, usually with a hood, fastened with wooden or horn toggles: short pegs pushed through loops of cord.
The people legally responsible for running a charity. Lanternline's want one search box by next month.
The Trust's typed-up case files, sighting reports and letters, searched by the assistant and by the old keyword box.
The search tool Lanternline's volunteers have used since the spring. It does vector search only and shows the top 3.
Lanternline's search box from 2012: keyword search ranked by BM25. It was still on the server, unused, until Thursday.

Search by meaning: turn the search and every document into lists of numbers (embeddings) with the same model, then return the documents whose lists are closest, like finding the nearest houses on a map.
Search results in order, best first. A document's rank is its place in the list: 1 for first.
Running a keyword search and a vector search over the same documents and merging their results into one list.

A way to merge ranked lists by place: each document gets 1 / (k + rank) points from each list it is in, the points are added, and the merged list is sorted by the total. Like a race series scored by finishing places.
Merging several ranked lists into one. Reciprocal rank fusion is one method; weighted blending is another.
The single ranked list fusion produces from the keyword and vector lists.

The fixed number in reciprocal rank fusion's 1 / (k + rank). A larger k shrinks the gap between first place and the places below. 60 in the 2009 paper and in Elasticsearch. Not the k in top-k, or BM25's k1.
How many top results from each list take part in the merge, like taking only the top 10 runners from each race. A document outside a list's window gets no points from that list.
Merging by score instead of place: shrink each search's scores to the same range, multiply each by a weight, and add them. The weights need tuning: trying values until results look right.
The range a search's scores fall in. Cosine similarity stays between -1 and 1; BM25 has no fixed top: 12.81 for her file on Conal's search.
A label that names one thing exactly, such as a case number, an error code or a surname. Close isn't good enough, the way a nearly right phone number rings a stranger.
The same meaning in other words: a mustard duffel coat for a yellow raincoat, Garrow Head for St Cleave's Light.
A test question whose right result is marked in advance, so a search can be checked against it. A retrieval test set is made of them.
Six questions with known right files: two names, two case numbers and two descriptions. In the sim a name or number passes when its file comes first, a description in the top 3.
A document one search ranks first with good reason, such as the only file holding a searched case number.
The sim's ten documents copied from the Lanternline archive. Every score in the sim is computed over these ten alone.

The sim's five numbers per document, set by hand, each for one idea: a case file, a name like Gor-, a yellow coat, the coast and the lighthouse, someone waiting at home. Real embeddings' numbers have no names.
In the sim, files with equal fused scores are ordered by the better keyword rank, then the better vector rank. Real systems may break ties differently.
A second, slower look at the top results of a search, scoring each against the question to put them in a better order. Case 5 of this season covers it.
A model that reads a question and one document together and scores how well they match, like a judge holding two pages side by side. Used for reranking.
A free add-on for the PostgreSQL database (a widely used program for storing data) that lets it store embeddings and find the closest ones.
PostgreSQL's built-in keyword search: it cuts text into searchable words and ranks the matches. pgvector's README pairs it with vector search for hybrid search.

Elasticsearch's name for one step of a search that returns a ranked list. A standard retriever does keyword search, a knn (nearest-neighbour) retriever does vector search, an RRF retriever merges them.
Elasticsearch's name for k in reciprocal rank fusion. It defaults to 60.
Elasticsearch's name for the rank window. The RRF retriever's reference gives a default of 10.
The main yearly research conference on information retrieval, the study of search, run by the ACM, a computing society. The RRF paper appeared at SIGIR 2009.
A method for merging rankings by majority vote between each pair of documents. The 2009 paper found RRF beat it.
An information retrieval system: anything that searches documents and ranks them, such as a search engine.
A short code a system shows when something fails, such as TS-999 in Anthropic's example. An exact identifier.
A written set of steps for handling a known problem or warning, like a recipe card, kept for the engineer on call.
The exact name a monitoring program gives a warning it raises, which the engineer on call that night then searches for in the runbooks.
The steps that cut text into words (tokens) for keyword search, such as making letters lower case. Changing it changes what matches, so the test set should be rerun.
Stock keeping unit: a shop's code for one product, such as a size and colour of one shirt. An exact identifier.
A rule in ISO/IEC 27001:2022's list of security controls (Annex A, 8.10): information held in systems and devices is deleted when no longer required, in every copy.
The international standard for keeping a company's information safe. Its Annex A lists controls, specific safeguards, that an outside auditor checks.
The international standard for how a company makes sure its work is done well. Clause 7.5.3 covers keeping records findable and fit to use.

atWork: Find a search at work that matches by embeddings alone: a support bot over tickets (customers' problem reports), an internal knowledge search, or a helper for the engineer on call that searches runbooks, the written steps for known problems. A common incident: an internal support search can't find tickets by error code, because every code embeds close to every other code, until keyword search is added beside the vectors and the two lists are fused. Try your own search with an exact identifier, such as an error code, an order number or a person's surname, and then with a description in other words. Does each come back where it should? Write a small test set with both kinds, names, codes and descriptions, with the right result marked, and run it whenever the window, k, the model or the analyzer changes. Standards-readiness note: if your company holds or is pursuing ISO 9001:2015 certification, clause 7.5.3 asks that documented information be available and suitable for use where and when it is needed, and a search that can't return a record by its own reference is the kind of gap an auditor raises. If it is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, a keyword index is a second copy of every document, so control A.8.10 (information deletion) applies to it too: make sure a deletion reaches both indexes, from the first build rather than at audit time. In the crossover season, Nightwatch's Build Night X1 builds an incident copilot, an assistant for outages, with RAG over runbooks: it searches them first and answers from what it finds. Its runbook search should be hybrid, because alert names, the exact names of warnings, are exact strings of letters.

recall.prompt: Your company's internal support search uses embeddings only. Engineers who paste in E-4031 get tickets about E-4013, E-4301 and other look-alikes, and the ticket that names E-4031 comes back fifth. Searches that describe the symptom in their own words work well. What is going on, and what do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: An embedding blurs an exact code, which carries little meaning, so look-alike codes rank above the exact match
Keep the vectors and add keyword search (BM25) beside them, so both searches run
Merge the two ranked lists by rank, for example with reciprocal rank fusion
Check it with a test set of known questions of each kind: codes and descriptions

recall.model: The search embeds E-4031, and a code like that carries little meaning, so its embedding lands among look-alike codes; the exact match is fifth because embeddings blur exact strings while handling the symptom descriptions well. Keep the vectors and add keyword search with BM25 beside them, so both searches run on every query: BM25 gives a rare token such as 4031 a heavy weight and puts the ticket that contains it first. Merge the two ranked lists with reciprocal rank fusion, each ticket scoring 1 / (60 + rank) from each list over a window of about 10 from each, so the exact match and the good descriptions both rise. Then write a test set of known questions with the right tickets marked, error codes and symptom descriptions, check that a code comes back first, and rerun it whenever the window, k or the model changes.

recall.prompt: Reciprocal rank fusion with k = 60. File A is first in the keyword list and outside the vector list's window. File B is fifth in both lists. Which comes first in the fused list?
options: File A: 1/61 is about 0.0164, and B gets 1/65, about 0.0154
They tie, because one first place is worth two fifth places
File B: 2/65 is about 0.0308, against A's 1/61, about 0.0164
File A, because a first place always beats any lower places
recall.why: B gets 1/65 from each list, 2/65, about 0.0308. A gets 1/61 from the keyword list and nothing from the vector list, about 0.0164. A file present in both lists usually beats a sure hit present in one, which is why a window too small to hold the sure hit in the second list can bury it, and why a test set with exact names and numbers should check that they still come first.

recall.prompt: A teammate proposes merging the keyword and vector results by adding each document's BM25 score to its cosine similarity and sorting by the total. On Conal's description the scores were BM25 12.81, 3.44, 2.35, 2.30 and 1.53, and cosine 0.997 for the sighting. What would you tell them?

keyIdeas.idea: The two scores are on different scales: BM25 is unbounded and runs to 12.81, while cosine stays at or below 1, so BM25 swamps the vectors
Merge by rank with reciprocal rank fusion, or normalize the scores and tune weights
Check whichever merge with a known-answer test set before it ships

recall.model: The two scores are on different scales: BM25 has no fixed top and runs to 12.81 here, while cosine similarity can't pass 1, so adding them lets BM25 swamp the vectors and the sum behaves almost like keyword search alone. The sighting would get 1.53 + 0.997 = 2.53 and still sit under files that only share common words. Merge by rank instead, with reciprocal rank fusion, which needs no common scale; or normalize each search's scores to a shared range and tune weights, which takes more work. Either way, run a known-answer test set with names, numbers and descriptions before it ships.

recall.prompt: A caller gives a missing person's rare surname and case number. Which search is usually most likely to put the right case file first?
options: Keyword search with BM25, because the rare tokens weigh most
Vector search, because embeddings understand what names mean
Vector search with a bigger embedding model and more dimensions
Either one, since a case number reads the same to both of them
recall.why: A rare surname and a case number are exact identifiers with little meaning. BM25 gives rare tokens high inverse document frequency, so the one file that holds them scores far above the rest, 4.99 and alone for Gorrimer 98/0417. An embedding places them near names and numbers that look alike, which is how her file came fourth. A hybrid search keeps both strengths.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. The hybrid box has run since November and Zillah's questions, now 40 of them, all passed. Last week a volunteer who codes swapped Bryher's merge for something he called simpler: add each file's keyword score to its vector score and sort by the total. Tonight Conal typed the yellow raincoat description again. The Saltrigg report came fifth, at 2.53. Above it: her file at 13.52, the letter of 2003 at 3.54, Wilfrida Gorringe's file at 2.68 and Lachlan Hartsop's at 2.63. The change went live on Friday, and nobody ran the questions.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did the Saltrigg report sink, and what should they do?

keyIdeas.idea: The keyword scores and the cosines are on different scales; BM25 runs far above 1 and swamps the cosine, so the sum acts like keyword search alone
Go back to merging by rank with reciprocal rank fusion, or normalize the scores and tune weights
Run the known-answer questions before every change goes live; a description question would have caught this

coldCase.model: Adding the scores mixed two scales. BM25 has no fixed top: her file scores 12.81 and the report only 1.53, while cosine similarity can't pass 1, so the report's 0.997 can never catch up and the sum behaves like keyword search alone: 1.53 + 0.997 = 2.53, fifth, under files that share only common words. Go back to merging by rank with reciprocal rank fusion, k = 60 and a window of 10, where the report comes second at 0.0318; or normalize each search's scores and tune weights, which needs more care. And run the test set of known answers before every change goes live: Zillah's description questions would have failed on Friday, before any caller did.

sources.title: Gordon V. Cormack, Charles L. A. Clarke and Stefan Büttcher, Reciprocal Rank Fusion outperforms Condorcet and individual Rank Learning Methods, SIGIR 2009 (RRFscore(d) = sum over rankings of 1 / (k + r(d)); k = 60 was fixed during a pilot investigation and not altered during subsequent validation; the constant k mitigates the impact of high rankings by outlier systems; k = 60 was near-optimal, but the choice was not critical)

Elastic, Elasticsearch reference, Reciprocal rank fusion, read 11 October 2026: RRF is a method for combining multiple result sets; rank_constant defaults to 60; rank_window_size determines the size of the individual result sets per query; a higher value will improve result relevance at the cost of performance

Elastic, Elasticsearch reference, RRF retriever, read 11 October 2026: rank_constant defaults to 60; rank_window_size defaults to 10; example combining a standard retriever with a knn retriever using RRF

Anthropic, Introducing Contextual Retrieval, published 19 September 2024, read 11 October 2026: BM25 uses lexical matching to find precise word or phrase matches; it's particularly effective for queries that include unique identifiers or technical terms; example Error code TS-999
pgvector README (GitHub), Hybrid Search, read 11 October 2026: use together with Postgres full-text search for hybrid search; you can use Reciprocal Rank Fusion or a cross-encoder to combine results
ISO 9001:2015, Quality management systems, Requirements: clause 7.5.3, control of documented information
ISO/IEC 27001:2022, Information security management systems, Requirements: Annex A control 8.10, information deletion
